opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the framing comes from an analogy with model merging. In the model merging literature, people take two networks trained on different tasks, sometimes just averaging or adding their weights, and end up with one network that can do both. If you take that idea seriously, you can imagine any trained network as having been built by adding together a bunch of simpler networks, each implementing its own little mechanism. Model unmerging asks: can we run that process in reverse? Given the final weights, can we recover the components that were summed together to produce them?

That's the core idea behind parameter decomposition, the line of work we've been pursuing with attribution-based parameter decomposition and more recently stochastic parameter decomposition. Instead of looking for features in activation space, which is what sparse autoencoders do, we decompose the parameters themselves. We look for a set of parameter components that sum to the original weights, so the decomposition is faithful to the actual network, and we want as few of those components as possible to matter on any given input, so the decomposition is sparse in how it's used. We also want each component to be as simple as possible, ideally low-rank.

The reason this appeals to me is that it gets at mechanisms rather than representations. An activation tells you what the network is representing at a point in the forward pass, but the computation lives in the weights. If you can carve the weights into pieces where each piece is responsible for one coherent bit of computation, and on any input only a handful of those pieces are doing anything, then you have a description of the network that is both faithful and much easier to understand. You can ablate the pieces that shouldn't matter on an input and the output doesn't change, which is the test you'd want for whether you've really separated the computations.

It also sidesteps some of the awkwardness we ran into with activation-based methods: questions about which layer to train on, feature splitting, and the gap between the features you find and the actual computation that uses them. Here the object of study is the mechanism itself. There are still hard problems, especially scaling these methods and making the optimization well-behaved, but conceptually, thinking of a network as a merge of many small mechanisms that we're trying to unmerge has been a clarifying way to think about what interpretability is ultimately after.

r001.rationale: The response discusses separating weight components, but does not describe an additional dimension beyond layers and neuron width.

r002.rationale: It presents a trained network as built by adding together simpler networks, each implementing its own mechanism, which conveys the combined-experts hypothesis.

r003.rationale: It describes reversing model merging to recover components, but does not say those components are networks that each perform as few tasks as possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about model unmerging starts from an observation about how we got here. For a few years, the dominant approach in mechanistic interpretability has been decomposing activations: you take the residual stream, train a sparse autoencoder or something similar, and hope the resulting directions correspond to meaningful concepts. That's been productive, but it has a structural problem. Activations are the wrong object. What we actually care about is the computation the network performs, and activations are just the intermediate state of that computation. Decomposing them tells you what the network is representing, not what it's doing with those representations.

Model unmerging reframes the question. Instead of asking "what directions live in this activation space," you ask "what if this network is really the sum of many smaller networks, each doing one thing, that happen to be overlaid on the same set of weights?" There's a nice intuition from model merging, where people take two fine-tuned models and add their weight deltas together and get a model that can do both tasks. Unmerging is the inverse. You take a single trained network and try to find a set of components in parameter space such that each component is, by itself, a complete mechanism, and together they reconstruct the original model's behavior.

Concretely, the way we operationalize this is to parametrize a set of components whose weights sum to the original weights, and then train them with two pressures. One is faithfulness: on any given input, the subset of components that are actually active needs to reproduce the network's output. The other is simplicity: we want as few components as possible to be active per input, and each component to be as low-rank or as simple as we can get away with. The hope is that the thing that falls out of that optimization is the network's actual mechanistic decomposition, because the true mechanisms are the cheapest way to explain the behavior.

What I find compelling about this compared to activation-based methods is that the components come with their own causal story built in. A component isn't a direction you then have to go and figure out how the network uses; it's a piece of the weights, so it already tells you what it reads from and what it writes to. You can ablate it cleanly. You can ask whether it's used on this input and not that one. And it handles things that activation decompositions struggle with, like features that are computed across multiple layers or that only make sense in terms of what they do rather than what they look like.

I'll be honest that it's early. The faithfulness-versus-simplicity tradeoff is delicate, there are hyperparameters that matter a lot, and we've mostly validated on toy models where we know the ground truth. Scaling to frontier models is the real test. But I think the conceptual shift, from decomposing representations to decomposing computations directly in parameter space, is the right direction, and it's the one I'd bet on.

r001.rationale: The response describes components in parameter space, but does not identify an additional dimension beyond the network’s layer and neuron-width coordinates.

r002.rationale: It frames the network as a sum of many smaller networks, each doing one thing, overlaid on shared weights.

r003.rationale: It calls unmerging the inverse of model merging and describes decomposing one network into components that are active selectively and perform distinct mechanisms.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about model unmerging is to start with the reverse operation: model merging. You can take networks that do different things and combine their parameters to get a network that, hopefully, does several of those things. Unmerging asks: given a network that already does lots of things, can we find components that could have been merged to produce it?

Those components wouldn’t necessarily correspond to separate groups of neurons. They might overlap in the neurons they use, but represent different computations. So you’re trying to find a decomposition of the network’s weights that gives you meaningful computational pieces.

The important qualification is that merely decomposing the weights isn’t enough. There are lots of mathematically valid ways to do that which wouldn’t explain anything. You want the components to have coherent functions, and you want to be able to test that causally: if you remove or change one component, does the behavior you associate with it change in the way you’d expect?

So the hope is to move from identifying features—things a model represents—to separating out the mechanisms that actually do something with those representations. That could give us a more useful level of abstraction for understanding how a network works.

r001.rationale: It says components may overlap in the neurons they use, but does not describe distinguishing computations along a dimension beyond layer and neuron-width coordinates.

r002.rationale: It presents the idea that networks doing different things can be combined into one network, and that unmerging seeks the component networks that could have been combined.

r003.rationale: It describes reversing model merging, but does not say the decomposition should yield networks that each perform as few tasks as possible.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about model unmerging is to start with the idea that a neural network might be doing lots of different computations using overlapping sets of parameters. So the boundaries between those computations aren’t necessarily visible in the architecture. You can’t just point to a layer and say, “That’s one algorithm, and the next layer is another algorithm.”

Model merging gives us a useful way to turn that problem around. If you can take several models and combine their weights into one model, could you take a trained model and find component models that, when merged, reconstruct it? That’s the basic intuition behind unmerging.

But reconstruction alone isn’t enough. There are lots of arbitrary ways to split up a set of weights. What you want is a decomposition where the components correspond to coherent computations, and where you can intervene on those components to understand what they contribute. If you remove one, does a particular capability disappear? If you change it, does the model’s behavior change in a predictable way?

So the ambition is to move from identifying individual features to separating the mechanisms that use those features. And the important caveat is that finding a mathematical decomposition doesn’t automatically mean you’ve discovered the actual computational structure. That’s something you have to test.

r001.rationale: It says computations may overlap and lack visible layer boundaries, but does not describe separating them along an additional dimension beyond layer and neuron-width coordinates.

r002.rationale: It describes recovering component models from a merged model, but does not present the network as a mixture of experts whose experts have been combined.

r003.rationale: It frames unmerging as recovering component models, but does not say that a many-task network is decomposed into networks performing as few tasks as possible.
